contents: Platform & pipelines Built and operate an on-premises Argo Workflows / K3s Kubernetes platform (~21 nodes plus a Slurm controller, 22 workflow templates, 10 scheduled jobs) that runs everything from demultiplexing to delivery. Automated demultiplexing and run-level QC across Illumina, PacBio, ONT, 10x Genomics, and AVITI, and automated project intake (n8n → Google Sheets → Argo API) with a YAML-driven report generator. Analyze a wide range of assays: bulk, BRB-seq, miRNA-seq, and single-cell RNA-seq; 16S/ITS and shotgun metagenomics; bacterial and phage hybrid assembly; variant calling for constructs; bisulfite methylation; HLA typing; CRISPR base-editing quantification; BCR repertoires. Advise investigators on experimental design, statistical power, batch confounding, and multiple-testing control, turning sequencing constraints into clear analysis strategies and interpretable results. Methods & quality Built a false-positive control for novel miRNA discovery: a 29,975-interval negative set that exposed snoRNA and scaRNA artifacts scoring as top “novel miRNAs”, which the standard checks missed. Benchmarked platforms and settings: shotgun vs 16S vs Nanopore microbiome profiles, BRB-seq vs mRNA-seq, AVITI demultiplexing filters, and the in-house Argo RNA-seq pipeline vs nf-core/rnaseq (~25–40 vs ~50–80 min per sample). Caught silent failures that produced no pipeline errors: a wrong bacterial strain reference, an adapter-dimer library reported as “100% mapped”, diploid variant calling applied to haploid constructs, and an overwritten miRNA reference. Recovered phage genomes under ~600:1 host contamination by designing a host-depletion hybrid assembly pipeline (Illumina/Element + Nanopore). Team & documentation Authored the team’s daily-operations SOP, built a 269-page internal knowledge base across 30+ analysis areas, created an RNA-seq workshop, and designed the scRNA-seq technical assignment used to hire bioinformatics candidates. contents: Liver fibrosis triage (first-author poster, SLM 2026) Co-developed a non-invasive fibrosis triage system that works from routine serum labs and returns a refer/clear decision for second-line testing. Designed in three layers: deterministic clinical scores (FIB-4, APRI, NFS, a metabolic-evidence score), per-patient guideline retrieval so every call cites guideline text, and nearest-neighbour grounding followed by LLM staging. Safety by design: the referral decision is written only by deterministic code, and automated tests enforce that the language model has no path to change it. My components: the deterministic triage pathway, the metabolic-risk layer, the kNN model, the validation runs, and the API. Population cohort engineering Built the analysis-ready NHANES 2017–March 2020 dataset: 15,560 participants × 108 variables joined from ~28 CDC files, with derived clinical indices (FIB-4, APRI, NFS, HOMA-IR, eGFR, ASCVD risk) and elastography-based fibrosis stages. Designed leak-free reference and test splits, kept the 2021–2023 cycle separate for independent validation, and harmonized NHANES with external cohorts from India and Iran. Transcriptomics & multimodal ML HCC multimodal fusion (first-author poster, ICGM 2026): combined an autoencoder pretrained on ARCHS4 liver RNA-seq, MedCLIP CT-image embeddings, and BioClinicalBERT clinical features for HCC classification. Integrated TCGA-LIHC mRNA and miRNA data into a regulatory network of inversely regulated miRNA–target pairs, followed by pathway analysis. Ran a multi-cohort replication study of MASH liver transcriptomes from public GEO data, adding cell-type deconvolution and DNA methylation. Analyzed single-cell and single-nucleus liver fibrosis data with pseudobulk DESeq2, testing robustness across 150 models (cell types × contrasts × covariates). Contributed to the comorbidity transcriptomics model (ICGM 2026), an NIH grant proposal on foundational AI models for fatty liver disease biomarkers, and a NAFLD/NASH meta-analysis review. contents:
Most RNA-seq problems are not hidden. They show up in the QC report, in the PCA plot, or in the p-value histogram. They just get skipped because the pipeline finished without errors and the volcano plot looks reasonable.
A finished pipeline is not a validated dataset. Below are the signals I check before trusting any result, grouped by the stage where they appear. None of the thresholds are universal. They depend on organism, tissue, and library prep. The point is to know what normal looks like for your setup, so that abnormal stands out.
1. Raw reads Quality that drops early in the read. A gradual quality decline toward the 3′ end is normal for Illumina. A sharp drop in the middle of the read, or spikes of N calls across many samples, points to an instrument or run problem, not a biology problem. Check whether it affects one lane or the whole run.
High adapter content. Adapters appear when the insert is shorter than the read length. A little is fine and trimming handles it. A lot usually means short fragments, which often means degraded RNA or over-fragmentation.
A shifted or bimodal GC distribution. Your samples should share a similar, roughly unimodal GC curve. A second peak suggests contamination, such as bacterial DNA, rRNA, or adapter dimers. Overrepresented sequences in FastQC often tell you which.
Duplication, read carefully. High duplication is expected in RNA-seq, because highly expressed genes generate many identical reads. It becomes a red flag when it comes with low input, low library complexity, and a flat expression profile. Tools like dupRadar separate expression-driven duplication from PCR artifacts. If the library has UMIs, deduplicating on them makes the distinction much clearer.
2. Alignment and quantification Low unique mapping rate. For a well-annotated organism such as human or mouse, a uniquely mapped rate well below your usual range is the first thing to investigate. Common causes are the wrong reference or annotation version, contamination, or a large rRNA fraction. Take a sample of the unmapped reads and check what they actually are, for example with FastQ Screen or a quick BLAST.
Strandedness mismatch. This one is quiet and costly. If a stranded library is counted as unstranded, or with the wrong strand setting, counts can drop by roughly half and antisense signal leaks into your genes. Confirm the library type instead of assuming it:
STAR’s ReadsPerGene.out.tab reports counts for all three strand settings side by side Salmon with -l A infers the library type and records it in lib_format_counts.json RSeQC’s infer_experiment.py reports the fraction of reads on each strand High intronic or intergenic reads. In a poly(A) library, a large intronic fraction suggests genomic DNA contamination or a lot of unspliced pre-mRNA. In total RNA or single-nucleus data, a higher intronic fraction is expected. Context decides whether this is a problem.
3′ bias in gene body coverage. In poly(A)-selected libraries, coverage piling up at the 3′ end is a classic sign of RNA degradation. Compare it against RIN values if you have them. In 3′-tag methods such as QuantSeq or BRB-seq, the same pattern is the design, not a defect.
rRNA and mitochondrial fractions. High rRNA means depletion or poly(A) selection did not work well. Mitochondrial reads vary by tissue: heart and muscle are naturally high. What matters is a sample that is far above its own group.
3. Sample level Library sizes that differ by an order of magnitude. Normalization handles moderate differences. Very uneven depth reduces power for the shallow samples, and can make them look like outliers for technical reasons alone.
PCA that separates by batch instead of biology. Color the PCA by every metadata column you have: prep date, lane, RIN, library size, operator. If PC1 lines up with prep date rather than condition, the batch effect is stronger than your biology. If batch and condition are perfectly confounded, no statistical correction can separate them.
One sample that does not belong. A sample-to-sample correlation heatmap makes outliers obvious. Before removing one, find out why it is different, and record the decision.
Sex genes that disagree with the metadata. Plot XIST against Y-linked genes such as RPS4Y1, DDX3Y, and KDM5D. A sample labeled female that expresses Y genes is a sample swap until proven otherwise. This takes five minutes and catches mistakes that no other QC step will.
Marker genes that point the wrong way. If your knockdown target is not reduced, or a treatment-response gene moves in the opposite direction, stop there. One caveat: in some knockout designs the transcript is still produced but missing the deleted exons, so check exon-level coverage before concluding the knockout failed.
4. Differential expression results The p-value histogram. Under a well-behaved test, it should be roughly flat, with a spike near zero for the genes that are actually changing. A hump in the middle or a strong slope suggests the model does not fit the data, often because of unaccounted batch structure or overdispersion. A spike near 1 often comes from low-count genes and largely disappears with independent filtering. This plot takes one line of code and is the most underused diagnostic in RNA-seq.
Thousands of DE genes from a mild treatment. Sometimes the biology really is that strong. More often it is a batch effect aligned with the condition, or a global shift in composition that the normalization assumption does not handle.
Zero DE genes. Before concluding there is no effect, check power (two replicates per group is very little), the design formula, and the contrast. Then check the contrast direction again.
Top hits dominated by mitochondrial, ribosomal, or hemoglobin genes. These usually reflect sample quality or tissue composition, such as blood contamination, rather than the treatment.
Huge fold changes on low-count genes. A gene going from 1 to 8 reads is a 3-log2 fold change with almost no information behind it. Use fold-change shrinkage, such as lfcShrink with apeglm in DESeq2, before ranking genes or sending results for enrichment.
An asymmetric volcano plot. A strongly lopsided volcano can be real, but it can also mean a global expression shift that violates the assumption that most genes do not change. Check the MA plot and the normalization factors before interpreting it.
A short checklist Stage Check Quick tool Raw reads Quality, adapters, GC, overrepresented sequences FastQC, MultiQC Alignment Unique mapping, strandedness, read distribution, gene body coverage STAR logs, Salmon, RSeQC, Qualimap Samples Library size, PCA by metadata, correlation heatmap, sex genes DESeq2 vst + PCA, heatmap DE p-value histogram, MA plot, fold-change shrinkage, contrast direction DESeq2, edgeR A QC report does not tell you that a dataset is good. It tells you where to look. The red flags above are not reasons to discard data. They are questions that need an answer before the results go into a figure, a report, or a decision.
title: RNA-seq Red Flags: What to Check Before You Trust Your Results

contents:
Differential expression analysis tells us which genes change between two conditions, but a list of genes is rarely enough on its own. Individual genes are noisy and hard to interpret without a broader framework.
Gene set enrichment analysis asks a different question: are the genes belonging to a known pathway systematically shifted toward the top or bottom of a genome-wide ranked list? This matters because many real biological processes involve coordinated but moderate changes across hundreds of genes rather than a few dramatic ones — exactly the pattern a significance threshold discards. This workflow runs RNA-seq differential expression results against four MSigDB collections using fgsea.
Why Not Just a Filtered Gene List? Over-representation analysis starts by filtering, say to padj < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1, then asks whether a pathway contains more of those genes than chance would predict. It has three weaknesses: it depends on an arbitrary cutoff (0.049 is in, 0.051 is out), it throws away ranking information entirely, and it favours large well-annotated pathways.
GSEA uses every gene that passes basic quality filtering. Each gene gets a ranking statistic and gene sets are tested for enrichment at the extremes of that ranking. Here the statistic is the stat column from DESeq2 — the Wald statistic — which is a good choice because it carries both effect size and uncertainty. Ranking by fold change alone over-prioritises noisy low-count genes; ranking by p-value alone loses direction.
Input and the Ranked Gene List The workflow expects a tab-delimited differential expression table with gene, stat, log2FoldChange, and padj columns, and filters out rows with missing values in critical fields. The central object is the ranked vector:
gene_rank <- res_df$stat names(gene_rank) <- res_df$gene gene_rank <- sort(gene_rank, decreasing = TRUE) Genes at the top are most strongly associated with the test condition; genes at the bottom with the control.
Everything downstream depends on the direction of the original contrast. If the comparison is test_vs_control, a positive enrichment score means the pathway is enriched in the test condition. Run the contrast the other way and every interpretation inverts. This is not a labelling nicety — it can flip the biological conclusion completely, so state the contrast explicitly in any report.
Before trusting pathway results, sanity-check the input: print the gene count and the top up- and downregulated genes. If known markers point the wrong way, stop there.
MSigDB Collections The workflow uses msigdbr to pull four collections, each a different kind of biological knowledge:
Collection Contents Best used for Hallmark Compact, curated sets for major processes (EMT, hypoxia, interferon response, cell cycle) First-pass interpretation — minimal redundancy, cleanest view of dominant programs C2 Curated pathways from KEGG, Reactome, BioCarta Mechanistic detail; more granular but often redundant across sources C3 Transcription factor and microRNA target signatures Hypotheses about upstream regulators C5 Gene Ontology terms (BP, MF, CC) Broad themes; heavily overlapping, needs summarising Two cautions. C3 enrichment does not demonstrate transcription factor activity — it generates a hypothesis to be checked against regulator expression, motif enrichment, chromatin data, or perturbation. And reporting a long table of significant GO terms is weak analysis; redundant terms should be grouped into higher-level themes.
Preparing Gene Sets for fgsea msigdbr returns one row per gene-to-set membership. fgsea wants a named list of gene vectors, so the table is grouped and collapsed:
gene_sets <- msigdb_data %>% dplyr::group_by(gs_name) %>% dplyr::summarize(genes = list(gene_symbol), .groups = "drop") %>% tibble::deframe() One gotcha worth fixing: deframe() lives in tibble. Calling it unqualified without loading the package fails with could not find function "deframe". Namespacing it, as above, makes the dependency explicit.
Running GSEA GSEA runs separately per collection:
fgsea( pathways = hallmark_sets, stats = gene_rank, minSize = 5, maxSize = 500, eps = 0 ) minSize and maxSize exclude sets that are too small to be stable or too broad to interpret. eps = 0 requests more accurate p-value estimation instead of stopping at a lower bound, at some cost in runtime.
Each result gives pathway, pval, padj, ES, NES, size, and leadingEdge. The normalized enrichment score is the most interpretable effect-size metric: positive means enrichment toward the top of the ranking, negative toward the bottom. Sets with padj < 0.05 are treated as significant.
What the Plots Show Hallmark — NES bar plot Significant Hallmark signatures ordered by NES, red for upregulated and blue for downregulated. A quick read on whether the dominant programs move up, down, or both.
Hallmark — NES vs significance NES against -log10(padj), which separates effect direction from strength of evidence. Dot size is gene set size.
C2 and C3 — top results Top significant curated pathways and regulatory target signatures, for mechanistic follow-up once the Hallmark picture is clear.
Enrichment score curves The top Hallmark pathway is HALLMARK_MYC_TARGETS_V1. The running score falls steadily to about -0.52 near rank 16,000, so MYC target genes sit toward the downregulated end. Tick marks show where the set’s genes fall in the ranking.
REACTOME_TRANSLATION, negatively enriched, minimum near -0.60 around rank 15,500. The ticks carry the story: translation genes are sparse at the upregulated end and dense past rank 16,000 — a coordinated shift across the whole set rather than a few outliers, which is precisely what threshold-based testing misses.
MIR6785_5P, worth contrasting with the others. The score is positive but weak, peaking near 0.19, and the ticks are spread almost uniformly across the ranking instead of concentrating at either end. This is what a large, diffuse set looks like when it reaches significance without a compelling directional signal — a reminder to read the curve, not just the adjusted p-value.
GOCC_RIBOSOMAL_SUBUNIT, the strongest of the four at about -0.72, and closely mirroring the C2 translation curve in both shape and trough position.
Read together, the curves make a coherent case: MYC targets down, translation down, ribosomal subunit down, all troughing in the same region of the ranking. That agreement is biologically sensible, since MYC directly drives ribosome biogenesis and translational capacity. Three collections describing one program at different resolutions is a far stronger result than any single striking curve — and the weak, diffuse C3 signature from the same run shows why the cross-collection check is worth doing.
Visualization is not interpretation, though. Significant pathways still have to make sense given the model system, tissue, treatment, and experimental design.
Leading Edge Genes The leading edge is the subset of genes driving the enrichment score, and it is where superficial pathway interpretation gets caught. Two pathways can share an NES but be driven by entirely different genes; conversely, several apparently distinct enriched pathways often share the same leading edge. If multiple immune pathways are significant on the same handful of genes, that is one infiltration program, not several independent mechanisms.
Quality Control GSEA is only as good as the ranked list and the annotation behind it. The recurring failure modes:
Identifier mismatch — this workflow assumes human gene symbols on both sides. Ensembl IDs, outdated symbols, or mouse genes give poor or misleading overlap. Duplicate symbols — GSEA needs one statistic per gene. Resolve duplicates deliberately, for example by keeping the strongest absolute statistic. Contrast direction — mislabel it and every up/down call inverts. Confounding — if batch, sex, donor, or run are not modelled in the differential expression step, GSEA will happily enrich technical artifacts. Redundancy — C2 and C5 produce many overlapping terms. Collapse them into themes. Version drift — MSigDB and gene symbols change. Record MSigDB version, package versions, R version, and the exact contrast. Before Production Use The script as written is a solid first-pass layer: it uses all genes, ranks by the signed statistic, covers four collections, and exports both tables and plots. A few changes would make it reproducible enough for production:
Move package installation out of the analysis script into renv, Conda, or a container. Record package and MSigDB versions alongside the results. Check for duplicate gene names before building the ranked vector, and report per-collection gene overlap. Export leading-edge genes, not only pathway-level summaries. Handle the empty case — plotting after filtering to padj < 0.05 can fail outright when nothing is significant. Results are exported per collection as CSVs (Hallmark, C2_CuratedPathways, C3_RegulatoryTargets, C5_GeneOntology) plus a summary counting significant sets per collection and direction.
Interpretation Order Confirm the contrast is what you think it is. Read Hallmark for broad programs. Refine with C2 curated pathways. Use C3 to generate upstream regulator hypotheses. Support themes with C5, without over-reading redundant terms. Inspect leading-edge genes across the top pathways. Connect back to the experimental system, phenotype, and metadata. This ordering guards against the most common mistake — treating a pathway name as a conclusion. An enrichment result is evidence that a defined gene set is non-randomly distributed in a ranked profile. It is not a mechanism, and mechanistic claims need more support.
Conclusion Ranking all genes by the signed differential expression statistic and testing curated MSigDB sets with fgsea detects coordinated programs that threshold-based gene list methods miss. Start with Hallmark, then go deeper with curated pathways, regulatory signatures, and GO terms.
Used carefully, this turns a flat differential expression table into a structured biological narrative. Used carelessly, it produces attractive plots with misleading interpretation. The difference is disciplined ranking, annotation control, reproducible execution, and honest review of contrast direction and leading-edge genes.
Additional Resources Complete Analysis Code: GSEA-MSigDB GitHub Repository MSigDB Collections: MSigDB Documentation fgsea Package: fgsea Documentation on Bioconductor clusterProfiler Package: clusterProfiler Documentation
title: From Differential Expression to Biological Signatures: A Practical GSEA Workflow Using MSigDB

contents:
Bulk RNA-seq deconvolution is a computational method for estimating which cell types are present in a mixed tissue sample, and in what relative amounts, from its combined gene expression profile.
In cancer research, it is mainly used to characterize the tumor microenvironment (TME): immune-cell infiltration, stromal composition, and, with appropriate reference data, malignant-cell populations.
The key point is that a tumor biopsy does not contain only cancer cells. It can contain malignant cells, T cells, B cells, macrophages, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and other populations. Standard bulk RNA-seq measures the combined RNA from all of them. Deconvolution tries to separate their contributions computationally.
1. What does deconvolution actually do? When you sequence a whole tumor sample, you get one gene expression profile, even though the tissue contains many cell types.
Deconvolution overview: a mixed tumor biopsy is sequenced as one bulk profile, compared with reference cell-type signatures, and turned into estimated cell-type fractions. Malignant cell Malignant cell Malignant cell Malignant cell Malignant cell Malignant cell Malignant cell Malignant cell Malignant cell Malignant cell Fibroblast Fibroblast Fibroblast Fibroblast T cell T cell T cell T cell T cell B cell B cell B cell Macrophage Macrophage Macrophage Tumor biopsy mixed cell types Bulk RNA-seq One mixed profile genes × samples Reference signatures T cells CD3D · CD3E · TRAC B cells MS4A1 · CD79A · CD79B + algorithm Compare with known cell-type profiles Estimated composition Malignant Malignant: 55% (hypothetical) 55% T cells T cells: 20% (hypothetical) 20% B cells B cells: 10% (hypothetical) 10% Macrophages Macrophages: 10% (hypothetical) 10% Fibroblasts Fibroblasts: 5% (hypothetical) 5% Cell-type fractions hypothetical output Figure 1. From a mixed biopsy to estimated cell-type fractions. The composition on the right is a hypothetical output, not measured data. Real values require a suitable, calibrated model. The algorithm compares the observed expression with reference expression patterns for individual cell types. For example, signatures that include CD3D, CD3E, and TRAC help identify T-cell contributions, while MS4A1, CD79A, and CD79B support B-cell identification. Each population needs a multigene signature, not a single marker.
A simplified version of the model is:
\[ Y_{g,s} \approx \sum_{k=1}^{K} S_{g,k}\, W_{k,s} + \epsilon_{g,s} \]where:
\(Y_{g,s}\) is the observed bulk expression of gene \(g\) in sample \(s\) \(S_{g,k}\) is the reference expression signature of cell type \(k\) \(W_{k,s}\) is the estimated contribution of cell type \(k\) to sample \(s\) \(\epsilon_{g,s}\) is unexplained expression and model error Depending on the method, \(W\) is an RNA contribution, a normalized cell fraction, or an enrichment score. These quantities are not interchangeable. A cell-type RNA fraction is not automatically the true percentage of cells in the tissue.
This framework underlies established methods such as CIBERSORT and CIBERSORTx [1, 2].
2. Why use deconvolution in tumor research? The main purpose is to separate changes in tumor-cell biology from changes in the cellular composition of the tissue.
Consider two tumors:
Tumor A: high malignant-cell content, few infiltrating immune cells Tumor B: lower malignant-cell content, substantial CD8 T-cell and macrophage infiltration Both produce bulk RNA-seq data, but the expression differences between them may be driven by their different cell populations rather than by transcriptional regulation inside the cancer cells. This is a major source of confounding in tumor differential expression analysis.
Analyses supported by deconvolution Analysis Question it answers Typical output Immune-cell profiling Which immune populations infiltrate each tumor? T-cell, B-cell, NK-cell, and myeloid estimates Tumor immune classification Are tumors immune-rich or immune-poor? Immune infiltration scores and clusters Stromal profiling Are fibroblasts or endothelial cells enriched? Stromal abundance estimates Tumor purity assessment What is the estimated malignant-cell contribution? Model-dependent purity estimate Group comparisons Is treatment or disease stage associated with immune composition? Effect sizes, confidence intervals, adjusted p-values Survival analysis Are cell populations associated with patient outcomes? Hazard ratios and survival associations Immunotherapy analysis Are immune populations associated with treatment response? Responder vs. non-responder differences Cell-type-specific expression Which cell type contributes to an expression signal? Inferred expression profiles per population These applications are supported by studies using CIBERSORTx, quanTIseq, EPIC, and BayesPrism [2–4, 9]. They produce estimates suitable for research analysis, not direct observations of each cell.
3. Which tools are available? Different tools answer different questions, and they should not be treated as interchangeable.
Tool Main purpose Output Best use in tumor studies CIBERSORT / CIBERSORTx [1, 2] Resolve immune subpopulations using signature matrices Relative fractions; CIBERSORTx also offers absolute-mode scores and inferred cell-type expression Detailed immune profiling EPIC [3] Quantify immune and stromal cells, with an uncharacterized compartment Estimated cell fractions Overall TME composition quanTIseq [4] Quantify ten immune cell types Fractions relative to all cells Tumor immune infiltration MCP-counter [5] Abundance of immune and stromal populations Scores in arbitrary units Comparing infiltration between samples xCell [6] Enrichment of many immune and stromal cell types Enrichment scores Broad immune and stromal screening TIMER [7] Selected immune populations with cancer-type-aware signatures Infiltration estimates Tumor immune association studies BayesPrism [9] Jointly infer composition and cell-type-specific expression from single-cell references RNA-contribution fractions and inferred expression Tumor heterogeneity and tumor–TME interactions Two distinctions matter most:
CIBERSORT relative fractions are not percentages of all tumor cells. With the LM22 reference, fractions are normalized across the 22 modeled leukocyte populations only. MCP-counter and xCell scores are not cell percentages. MCP-counter is designed to compare the same cell population across samples, and xCell returns enrichment scores. Their values cannot be compared directly across different cell types. How relative fractions can mislead Suppose two biopsies have these independently measured compositions:
Measure Tumor A Tumor B Immune cells among all tissue cells 2% 20% CD8 T cells among immune cells 50% 25% CD8 T cells among all tissue cells 1% 5% Relative versus absolute CD8 T-cell estimates. Among immune cells, Tumor A is 50% CD8 T cells and Tumor B 25%. Among all cells, Tumor A is 1% and Tumor B 5%. Relative to immune cells what a relative LM22 fraction reports Tumor A: 50% of immune cells 50% Tumor A Tumor B: 25% of immune cells 25% Tumor B Relative to all cells the abundance you usually want Tumor A: 1% of all cells 1% Tumor A Tumor B: 5% of all cells 5% Tumor B Figure 2. The same two tumors, two denominators. A relative immune-cell method ranks Tumor A higher; relative to all cells, Tumor B has five times the CD8 T-cell content. Values are hypothetical. A relative immune-cell deconvolution could report 50% CD8 T cells for Tumor A and 25% for Tumor B. But Tumor B actually has five times the proportion of CD8 T cells across all of its cells. Concluding that Tumor A has more CD8 T-cell infiltration from relative LM22 fractions alone would be wrong.
The distinction between within-sample and between-sample comparisons is discussed in detail in the benchmark by Sturm et al. [8], and it is why methods such as EPIC and quanTIseq estimate fractions relative to all cells, including an uncharacterized compartment [3, 4].
4. What does the output look like? For a cohort, the main output is usually a matrix with one row per sample and one column per cell population.
Hypothetical EPIC-like output, for illustration only:
Sample CD8 T CD4 T B cells Macrophages Other cells Tumor_01 0.08 0.05 0.03 0.09 0.75 Tumor_02 0.19 0.11 0.08 0.12 0.50 Tumor_03 0.02 0.03 0.01 0.04 0.90 Tumor_04 0.14 0.07 0.09 0.15 0.55 The “other cells” column can include malignant cells and any population not resolved separately. It must not automatically be labeled as tumor purity.

Other common outputs include immune-cell heatmaps, tumor-versus-normal comparisons, correlations between cell populations, treatment-associated changes, survival models, and cell-type-specific expression profiles when the algorithm supports them.
5. Important limitations in tumor samples Limitation Cause Consequence Missing cell types Reference does not represent every population Transcripts get assigned to the wrong populations Tumor-specific expression Malignant cells express genes that overlap immune or stromal signatures False or biased infiltration estimates Similar cell states Naive, activated, exhausted, and regulatory cells share many genes Poor resolution of closely related subtypes Tumor purity variation Different malignant-cell proportions shift bulk expression Apparent differences in immune populations or DEGs RNA content differences Cell types produce different amounts of RNA per cell RNA proportions differ from cell proportions Reference batch effects scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq measure expression differently Systematically biased estimates No spatial information Homogenization destroys tissue structure Cannot tell tumor-infiltrating cells from peripheral or TLS-localized ones The benchmark by Sturm et al. (2019) showed that accuracy varies substantially by cell type and reference signature. Methods do better for transcriptionally distinct populations than for closely related immune subsets [8].
Also note that the CIBERSORTx empirical p-value measures whether the reference-based fit beats a random baseline. It is not a p-value for a difference in cell abundance between groups [2].
6. A practical workflow for tumor bulk RNA-seq FASTQ → QC → alignment / quantification Normalized expression matrix: non-log values, normalized as the chosen tool expects Reference selection + deconvolution: CIBERSORTx, EPIC, quanTIseq, or BayesPrism Composition matrix + QC: reference coverage, model fit, purity, and agreement across methods Statistical and biological analysis: group comparisons, survival, immune signatures, integration with DEGs For CIBERSORTx, the published protocol uses TPM input and requires non-log, non-negative expression. Batch correction should match how the reference and mixture were generated; for example, signatures built from droplet-based scRNA-seq may need S-mode correction [10].
For a real tumor cohort, I would:
Estimate immune and stromal abundance with EPIC or quanTIseq. Run CIBERSORTx with LM22 for finer immune subpopulations, or with a tumor-matched single-cell reference when one is available. Check that the inferred populations agree with marker expression, pathology, and independent estimates. Compare populations between groups with appropriate covariate adjustment and FDR control, using compositional methods when modeling fractions. Integrate with bulk DEGs and pathway analysis, explicitly separating infiltration-driven expression changes from cell-intrinsic regulation. Deconvolution fractions should not automatically be added as covariates to every DE model. Whether to adjust depends on whether cell composition is a confounder or a biological consequence of the condition you are studying.
Bottom line Deconvolution turns bulk tumor RNA-seq into estimates of cellular composition. Its main value is showing how immune and stromal infiltration varies across patients, treatments, and outcomes, and helping separate composition effects from tumor-cell-intrinsic transcriptional changes.
For general tumor immune profiling, CIBERSORTx plus EPIC or quanTIseq gives complementary information. For tumor-cell-specific transcriptional programs, a suitable tumor-matched single-cell reference with BayesPrism or CIBERSORTx expression imputation is more appropriate.

contents:
You have run RNA-seq. You have fold changes, p-values, and maybe a volcano plot that looks perfect. Then comes the hard question:
What biology does this actually mean?
This is where functional enrichment comes in. Functional enrichment helps translate gene-level statistics into biological insight. The three names people usually hear are GO, KEGG, and GSEA. They are often treated as competitors, but in reality they do very different jobs.
Understanding how they differ makes enrichment analysis much easier and much more meaningful.
First, How Functional Enrichment is Actually Done In real RNA-seq workflows, enrichment is performed using two main statistical approaches:
Over-Representation Analysis (ORA) Functional Class Scoring (FCS), most commonly implemented as Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) Important distinction: GO and KEGG are not methods. They are collections of gene sets. ORA and GSEA are the methods used to test those gene sets.
Keeping this distinction in mind avoids most confusion.
GO Enrichment: What Do My Genes Do? Gene Ontology (GO) focuses on gene function. It describes what genes do, where they act, and which biological processes they belong to.
GO answers questions such as:
Which biological processes are changing? Which molecular functions are enriched? Where in the cell is activity occurring? GO is organized into three branches:
Biological Process (for example, immune response) Molecular Function (for example, kinase activity) Cellular Component (for example, mitochondrion) GO enrichment is most commonly performed using ORA. This means it uses a list of differentially expressed genes and asks whether certain GO terms appear more often than expected.
GO works best when you have a clear DEG list and want broad biological interpretation for a Results section.
A simple way to think about GO is that it provides the job descriptions of your genes.
KEGG Pathway Analysis: How Do Genes Work Together? KEGG looks at pathways rather than individual functions. These pathways include metabolic routes, signaling cascades, and disease-related networks.
Instead of abstract terms, KEGG gives concrete pathways such as glycolysis, MAPK signaling, or T-cell receptor signaling, often with diagrams showing how genes interact.
KEGG enrichment is also commonly performed using ORA. In this case, it asks whether a pathway contains more DEGs than expected.
KEGG is most useful when you want mechanistic insight and when pathway structure and gene interactions matter.
A helpful way to think about KEGG is as a wiring diagram of the cell.
GSEA: Are Pathways Shifting Even If No Genes Scream? Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) takes a completely different approach.
Instead of starting with a DEG list, GSEA uses all genes from the experiment, ranked by expression change. It then asks whether genes from a given pathway or functional group tend to appear near the top or bottom of that ranked list.
There are no hard cutoffs and no requirement for individual genes to be strongly significant.
GSEA is especially powerful when:
Fold changes are modest Few genes pass DEG thresholds Biology is driven by coordinated regulation rather than on-off changes A classic example is inflammation. Many inflammatory genes may change slightly, but together they form a strong biological signal that GSEA can detect even when ORA cannot.
A good way to think about GSEA is that it detects the overall state or mood of the transcriptome.
The Key Difference: ORA Versus GSEA The most important distinction is not GO versus KEGG versus GSEA. It is ORA versus GSEA.
ORA works by selecting a small set of genes and asking which pathways are over-represented. As a result, ORA results are usually driven by a small number of strongly changing genes.
GSEA works by examining all genes and asking whether many genes from the same pathway shift together. As a result, GSEA results are driven by dozens or hundreds of genes showing coordinated but modest changes.
This explains why GSEA often produces stronger and more consistent enrichment results than ORA in complex datasets.
Choosing the Right Tool Use GO enrichment when you want functional categories and broad biological summaries. Use KEGG enrichment when you want pathway-level mechanisms and interpretable diagrams. Use GSEA when changes are subtle, DEG lists are small, or you suspect system-level regulation. In practice, the best analyses do not choose one method. They combine them.
GO helps identify what functions are changing. KEGG helps explain how pathways are affected. GSEA reveals whether entire biological systems are shifting together. If GO is the dictionary, KEGG is the circuit diagram, and GSEA is the overall mood of the cell.
Using all three turns RNA-seq results from a list of genes into real biological understanding.
Practical Implementation I’ve created a comprehensive R workflow that implements all three enrichment methods side-by-side. This allows you to:
Compare results across methods to see which pathways each method identifies Understand the scale differences - ORA methods typically find pathways with 5-20 genes, while GSEA finds pathways with 50-200+ genes Get complementary insights - ORA finds specific “needles” while GSEA finds coordinated “haystacks” The workflow includes:
GO enrichment using ORA KEGG enrichment using ORA GSEA with GO gene sets GSEA with KEGG pathways Side-by-side comparison visualizations Publication-ready tables and plots Figure 1: Gene count distribution across enrichment methods. GSEA methods identify pathways with 10-20x more genes than ORA methods, reflecting their ability to capture coordinated changes across large gene sets.
Figure 2: P-value distribution comparison showing the significance of pathways identified by each method.
Key Insights from the Analysis Direct comparison of enrichment strategies revealed that DEG-based ORA and rank-based GSEA capture fundamentally different regulatory signals. While GO and KEGG ORA detected only a limited number of moderately significant terms, GSEA identified robust and highly significant enrichment across both ontologies and pathways. This discrepancy reflects a transcriptional landscape characterized by widespread, coordinated modulation of gene sets rather than isolated, high-magnitude gene expression changes. Consequently, GSEA provides a more sensitive and biologically informative representation of the underlying regulatory programs active in this condition.
Scale Differences ORA Methods: Typically identify pathways with 5-20 genes per term/pathway
Focused, specific biological functions Best for identifying key driver genes GSEA Methods: Typically identify pathways with 50-200+ genes per term/pathway
Broad, coordinated biological programs Best for detecting subtle but system-wide changes When to Use Each Method Use ORA methods when:
You have clear, strong differential expression You want to identify specific genes and functions You need focused, interpretable results Use GSEA methods when:
You have subtle but coordinated changes You want pathway-level insights You need to detect changes that might not pass strict DEG thresholds Complete Workflow Available on GitHub I’ve made the complete analysis workflow available on GitHub, including:
Full R Markdown analysis script Step-by-step documentation Example visualizations Comparison analyses All code is reproducible and well-documented 🔗 View the complete workflow on GitHub
The repository includes:
Complete R Markdown workflow Data preparation scripts Visualization code Results tables All generated plots and figures Conclusion Functional enrichment analysis is not about choosing one method over another. It’s about understanding what each method tells you and using them together to build a complete picture of your RNA-seq data.
GO tells you what functions are changing KEGG tells you how pathways are affected GSEA tells you whether entire systems are shifting Together, they transform a list of differentially expressed genes into meaningful biological insights.

contents:
Hi, I’m Kiran Adhikari, a bioinformatics scientist with a background in pharmaceutical sciences. I work at the intersection of biology, computational science, and medicine, using genomic data to investigate disease mechanisms, discover biomarkers, and explore potential therapeutic targets.
My work ranges from analyzing RNA-seq and single-cell datasets to developing bioinformatics pipelines that process millions of sequencing reads. I’m particularly interested in understanding what molecular data can tell us about disease, and just as importantly, what it cannot.
A little about my background My academic journey started in pharmacy. I completed my B.Pharm in Pharmacy and M.Pharm in Pharmaceutical Technology at Gujarat Technological University, India. My master’s research focused on developing a sustained-release formulation of favipiravir, an antiviral drug.
Before moving into bioinformatics, I worked at Accuprec Research Laboratories, an OECD GLP contract research organization, where I was involved in preclinical toxicology studies using animal models and cell lines. Working alongside pharmacologists, toxicologists, microbiologists, and veterinarians gave me firsthand experience with experimental research and drug safety evaluation.
During this work, I became interested in the molecular changes behind biological responses. Knowing whether a compound was toxic was important, but understanding which genes, pathways, and cellular processes were affected seemed equally valuable. This interest eventually brought me to bioinformatics.
I completed my M.S. in Bioinformatics at Hood College, Maryland, where I worked with Dr. Miranda Darby and Dr. Daniel Sierra-Sosa on splice-site prediction using RNA-seq data.
We developed splice-junction datasets from publicly available sequencing data and compared different machine-learning approaches. Interestingly, our neural network did not outperform a simpler linear model. It was a good lesson in why benchmarking matters and why more complex models are not always better. A manuscript from this work is currently in preparation.
What I do Most of my work involves applying computational methods to biological questions, often in collaboration with researchers from different scientific backgrounds.
At AmpSeq, I work with academic and government laboratories on projects involving transcriptomics, genomics, toxicology, infectious diseases, radiation biology, and stem-cell research.
My role goes beyond running analyses. I work with investigators on experimental design, data quality, statistical approaches, and biological interpretation. I also develop and maintain bioinformatics pipelines for large-scale sequencing datasets, using technologies such as Nextflow, Argo, Docker, Kubernetes, and HPC infrastructure.
Some days involve exploring gene-expression patterns or comparing cell populations. Others involve troubleshooting sequencing workflows, optimizing computational resources, or figuring out why a dataset behaves differently than expected. That variety is one of the things I like about bioinformatics.
At Karyon Bio, my research focuses on metabolic liver disease, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
I analyzed bulk and single-cell transcriptomic datasets to identify disease-associated gene signatures and investigate changes in liver cell populations. Much of this work involved comparing findings across independent patient cohorts to understand which molecular patterns were reproducible.
I also worked on machine-learning approaches for biomarker discovery and clinical prediction, including co-developing a decision-support tool to help identify patients who may benefit from additional liver fibrosis imaging.
This research contributed to two first-author conference presentations in 2026 at the Saudi Liver Meeting and ICGM. I also contributed to an NIH grant proposal focused on AI-based biomarker discovery in metabolic liver disease.
Earlier, at Cian Diagnostics, I worked on long-read sequencing, variant calling, and DNA methylation analysis, including research involving portable DNA sequencing technologies.
What interests me I’m interested in the connection between molecular data and disease biology.
Transcriptomics and other high-throughput technologies allow us to study thousands of genes and complex cellular systems, but finding a statistically significant result is only one part of understanding a disease. The more interesting questions often come afterward: Is the finding reproducible? Does it reflect a meaningful biological mechanism? Can it help identify a therapeutic target?
My interests extend to molecular pharmacology, neuroscience, and drug discovery, particularly understanding the molecular mechanisms of neurological and psychiatric disorders.
Having worked in both pharmaceutical research and computational biology, I would like to bring these areas closer together by combining computational findings with experimental approaches to target discovery and validation.
Tools I work with I use Python, R, Bash, and SQL for most of my computational work. My experience covers several areas of bioinformatics and biomedical research.
